## The brief is deliberately too large

```{=html}
<div class="stage opening-stage">
  <div>
    <div class="eyebrow">THE STARTING POINT</div>
    <p class="big-claim">Choose work that one agent cannot hold in its head.</p>
    <div class="metric-line"><b>Many</b><span>subsystems and platforms</span></div>
    <div class="metric-line"><b>Many</b><span>workers in parallel</span></div>
    <div class="metric-line"><b>One</b><span>coherent product</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="system-map" aria-label="A large product divided into architectural regions">
    <div class="map-node domain"><b>Domain</b><span>model · rules</span></div>
    <div class="map-node engine"><b>Engine</b><span>commands · state</span></div>
    <div class="map-node io"><b>Data</b><span>I/O · protocols</span></div>
    <div class="map-node ui"><b>Interface</b><span>desktop · web</span></div>
    <div class="map-node tools"><b>Automation</b><span>CLI · agents</span></div>
    <div class="map-node proof"><b>Evidence</b><span>tests · scorecards</span></div>
    <div class="map-center"><b>REPOSITORY</b><span>the shared model of reality</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The interesting swarm problems are too large for one worker to understand at once.  They cross subsystems, platforms, tools, and definitions of done.

The trick is not to give every agent more context.  The trick is to arrange the repository so that each agent needs less context, while the finished pieces still compose into one product.

This is an architectural problem before it is a prompting problem.
:::

## `AGENTS.md` is the control plane

```{=html}
<div class="stage document-stage">
  <div class="artifact paper">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>AGENTS.md</span><span>read first</span></div>
    <h3>One shared operating manual</h3>
    <div class="rule"><b>Orient</b><span>Architecture, roadmap, gaps, scorecard</span></div>
    <div class="rule"><b>Choose</b><span>Highest-ranked work that nobody owns</span></div>
    <div class="rule"><b>Build</b><span>One command, one module, one testable slice</span></div>
    <div class="rule"><b>Finish</b><span>Run the gates and leave a terse dev log</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="side-copy">
    <p class="big-claim compact">The prompt is part of the codebase.</p>
    <p>Every worker starts with the same map, rules, and definition of done.</p>
    <p class="accent-note">Less private context.  Fewer invented conventions.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The first artifact is the operating manual.  `AGENTS.md` is not a welcome note.  It records how work is chosen, where code belongs, which files are shared, how changes are validated, and what a clean handoff looks like.

That moves maintainer judgment out of private conversations and into versioned project state.  Every worker begins with the same rules, and the rules evolve with the software.

Specific instructions beat vague encouragement.  “Dependencies point down” and “new behavior gets a new module” are useful.  “Write good code” is not.
:::

## Architecture is a map of safe ownership

```{=html}
<div class="architecture-stage">
  <div class="layer-stack">
    <div class="layer l6"><b>L6</b><span>interfaces · automation</span></div>
    <div class="layer l5"><b>L5</b><span>application services · command registry</span></div>
    <div class="layer l4"><b>L4</b><span>adapters · storage · protocols</span></div>
    <div class="layer l3"><b>L3</b><span>compute · scheduling · composition</span></div>
    <div class="layer l2"><b>L2</b><span>domain algorithms</span></div>
    <div class="layer l1"><b>L1</b><span>domain model</span></div>
    <div class="layer l0"><b>L0</b><span>types · geometry · codecs</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="side-copy architecture-copy">
    <div class="eyebrow">ARTIFACT · architecture.md</div>
    <p class="big-claim compact">Dependencies may only point downward.</p>
    <p><code>check-layers</code> enforces the rule.  The diagram is not a suggestion.</p>
    <p class="accent-note">A worker can own one region without learning the entire system.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Parallel work needs boundaries that a machine can enforce.  The architecture document describes layers, allowed dependencies, public seams, and ownership zones.

A layer checker turns the diagram into a rule.  A worker changing storage cannot quietly reach into the interface.  A worker adding a command cannot bypass the domain model.

The architecture therefore does two jobs.  It keeps the software clean, and it reduces the amount of context needed to make a safe change.
:::

## The product surface is a contract

```{=html}
<div class="stage menu-stage">
  <div class="artifact code-paper">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>surface_catalog.toml</span><span>versioned</span></div>
    <div class="menu-row"><span>Workspace</span><b>Open</b><code>workspace.open</code></div>
    <div class="menu-row"><span>Document</span><b>Transform</b><code>document.transform</code></div>
    <div class="menu-row"><span>Data</span><b>Import</b><code>data.import</code></div>
    <div class="menu-row"><span>Output</span><b>Export</b><code>output.export</code></div>
  </div>
  <div class="menu-result">
    <div class="ring"><span>KNOWN</span><small>product surface</small></div>
    <p>Matching command found: enabled.<br>Missing implementation: visible, but incomplete.</p>
    <p class="accent-note">Ambition becomes a measurable backlog.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
A swarm needs a finite description of the product it is trying to build.  The surface catalog records every user-visible capability with a stable identifier.

Those identifiers join interface, engine, automation, documentation, and tracking.  When an implementation registers the identifier, every client can discover it.  When it is missing, the gap remains visible.

The catalog prevents a common failure mode: lots of locally impressive work with no reliable picture of whether the product is becoming complete.
:::

## Everything becomes one command

```{=html}
<div class="command-stage">
  <div class="artifact command-spec">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>CommandSpec</span><span>the application seam</span></div>
    <pre><code>id        "document.transform"
label     "Transform…"
params    { mode, amount }
enabled   has_active_document
run       transform_document
undo      restore_snapshot</code></pre>
  </div>
  <div class="clients">
    <div><b>Desktop</b><span>menu or gesture</span></div>
    <div><b>CLI</b><span>headless run</span></div>
    <div><b>Agent</b><span>structured tool</span></div>
    <div><b>Replay</b><span>recorded action</span></div>
  </div>
  <p class="command-caption">Four clients.  One behavior.  One undo boundary.</p>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The command registry is the central seam.  A command carries its stable ID, parameters, precondition, implementation, result, and undo behavior.

Every client converges on that registry.  The interface does not contain a second implementation.  The automation layer does not invent another API.  Recorded actions do not bypass validation.

This makes functionality composable.  It also gives agents a small, typed place to discover and extend behavior.
:::

## The backlog is executable

```{=html}
<div class="tracking-stage">
  <div class="tracking-doc road"><span>ROADMAP.md</span><b>What matters now?</b><small>stage · milestones · honest readiness</small></div>
  <div class="tracking-doc gaps"><span>docs/gaps.md</span><b>What should a worker pick?</b><small>ranked by user impact and dependency</small></div>
  <div class="tracking-doc score"><span>scorecard/*.toml</span><b>What counts as done?</b><small>status · issue · evidence · budget</small></div>
  <div class="tracking-doc report"><span>docs/scorecard.md</span><b>Does the report match reality?</b><small>generated · checked in CI</small></div>
</div>
<p class="tracking-caption">Strategy becomes a queue.  The queue becomes evidence.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
The work queue belongs in the repository too.  The roadmap says where the product is going.  The gaps document ranks missing behavior.  Machine-readable scorecards attach status, evidence, and budgets to individual capabilities.

A worker can choose useful work without a meeting.  More importantly, the same worker updates the evidence when the change lands.  CI regenerates reports and rejects stale claims.

This keeps the swarm aimed at user value rather than whatever task happens to be easiest to prompt.
:::

## The repository runs the swarm

```{=html}
<div class="swarm-stage">
  <div class="agent-field" aria-label="Several independent agents working around a shared repository">
    <span class="agent a1">A</span><span class="agent a2">A</span><span class="agent a3">A</span><span class="agent a4">A</span>
    <span class="agent a5">A</span><span class="agent a6">A</span><span class="agent a7">A</span><span class="agent a8">A</span>
    <div class="repo-core"><span class="repo-glyph">{ }</span><b>REPO</b><small>rules · queue · evidence</small></div>
  </div>
  <div class="swarm-rules">
    <div><b>Isolated workspaces</b><span>No shared build-state queue</span></div>
    <div><b>Explicit file ownership</b><span>Small edits to shared registries</span></div>
    <div><b>Additive modules</b><span>Parallel changes rarely collide</span></div>
    <div><b>Green handoffs</b><span>The next worker starts from a stable tree</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
There is no magical conductor in the middle.  The repository coordinates the swarm.

Workers use isolated workspaces, claim narrow file sets, add behavior in new modules, and keep edits to shared registries small.  The shared artifacts tell each worker what matters and what finished means.

This looks more like a distributed system than a group chat.  Workers do not need identical knowledge.  They need stable contracts, low-conflict write paths, and a reliable shared state.
:::

## Vertical slices keep merges boring

```{=html}
<div class="slice-stage">
  <div class="slice-list">
    <div><i>01</i><b>Choose one visible gap</b><span>One outcome, not a subsystem rewrite</span></div>
    <div><i>02</i><b>Add one command module</b><span><code>transform_command.rs</code></span></div>
    <div><i>03</i><b>Reuse the lower layer</b><span><code>domain::transform</code></span></div>
    <div><i>04</i><b>Prove failure and success</b><span>bad input · output · undo</span></div>
    <div><i>05</i><b>Raise the evidence</b><span>catalog · scorecard · dev log</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="slice-proof artifact">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>change set</span><span>small enough to review</span></div>
    <div class="proof-line add"><b>+</b><span>src/commands/transform.rs</span></div>
    <div class="proof-line add"><b>+</b><span>tests/transform_fixture.rs</span></div>
    <div class="proof-line edit"><b>±</b><span>src/commands/registry.rs</span></div>
    <div class="proof-line edit"><b>±</b><span>scorecard/capabilities.toml</span></div>
    <div class="proof-result"><span>tests</span><b>PASS</b><span>layers</span><b>PASS</b><span>evidence</span><b>UPDATED</b></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The unit of parallel work is a vertical slice, not a broad layer.  A useful slice starts with one visible gap, adds one command, reuses or extends a lower-level capability, proves success and failure, and updates the evidence.

That shape is easy to review and easy to merge.  It avoids the swarm failure where one worker builds a framework, another builds an interface, and neither quite matches the other.

Most files in the change are new.  Shared registries receive only the smallest possible edit.
:::

## Agents can operate the product

```{=html}
<div class="operate-stage">
  <div class="operate-code"><div class="artifact-bar"><span>agent control protocol</span><span>same command IDs</span></div><pre><code>command_list  { filter }
command_run   { id, params }
state_inspect { selection, history }
render_preview{ max_size }
ui_screenshot { live_window }</code></pre></div>
  <div class="observe-loop">
    <div><b>Inspect</b><span>state, commands, preconditions</span></div>
    <div><b>Act</b><span>the same application path as the UI</span></div>
    <div><b>See</b><span>bounded output or full screenshot</span></div>
    <div><b>Correct</b><span>use the returned error, not a guess</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="operate-caption">A bug report can become a runnable script.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Agents should be able to operate the software, not merely edit source and hope.  A small control protocol exposes the command catalog, preconditions, state, bounded previews, and interface screenshots.

The tools use the same command path as the human interface.  They do not create a privileged second application hidden behind the first.

This closes the loop: inspect, act, see, correct.  It also makes bug reports executable.  A reproduction can be a short command sequence rather than a paragraph about where somebody clicked.
:::

## Why Rust fits the framework

```{=html}
<div class="rust-stage">
  <div class="rust-word">Rust</div>
  <div class="rust-reasons">
    <div><b>One language</b><span>domain, native UI, CLI, automation, web build</span></div>
    <div><b>Explicit seams</b><span>types make architectural boundaries harder to blur</span></div>
    <div><b>Local reasoning</b><span>ownership exposes sharing and mutation</span></div>
    <div><b>Native speed</b><span>parallel CPU work and portable GPU compute</span></div>
    <div><b>Portable core</b><span>desktop platforms and WebAssembly</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The framework does not require Rust, but Rust reinforces its ideas unusually well.

Types make command and layer seams explicit.  Ownership makes sharing and mutation visible.  Errors are values rather than hidden control flow.  The domain, native interface, command-line tools, automation server, and browser build can live in one language and one workspace.

Rust does not make correctness automatic.  It does make many accidental forms of architectural drift harder to introduce across agent boundaries.
:::

## Tests and measures, not trust

```{=html}
<div class="qm-stage">
  <div class="qm-panel">
    <div class="eyebrow">TESTS · DOES IT BEHAVE?</div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Unit + property</b><span>every crate; generated inputs for the tricky data structures</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Round trips</b><span>read, write, compare byte for byte</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Hostile input</b><span>truncate at every offset; fuzz the parsers in CI</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Real files</b><span>pinned, checksum-verified corpora with pass floors</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Render oracle</b><span>compare output with the file's own embedded preview</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Agent tasks</b><span>realistic edits through the control API, checked by screenshot</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="qm-panel measures">
    <div class="eyebrow">MEASURES · HOW GOOD IS IT?</div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Perf budgets</b><span>named scenarios with targets; regressions fail</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Size gate</b><span>the web build must stay under its limit</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Coverage floor</b><span>the count of live commands can't go down</span></div>
    <div class="qm-row"><b>Scorecard</b><span>generated from evidence; CI fails if it's stale</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="qm-gates">Every change also passes <b>format</b> · <b>lint</b> · <b>layers</b> · <b>cross-target builds</b></p>
```

::: {.notes}
The swarm expects workers to make mistakes, so quality has to be checked by machines, not assumed.  There are two kinds of check.

Tests answer "does it behave?".  Every crate has unit tests, with property tests generating inputs for the trickiest data structures.  File formats get byte-exact round trips, and hostile input: files truncated at every offset, plus fuzz targets for the parsers that run in CI.  Real-world files live in pinned, checksum-verified corpora, and the pass counts have floors that can't drop.  A render oracle compares the compositor's output with the image the file itself embeds.  And a set of realistic agent tasks drives the app through the control API and checks the result by screenshot.

Measures answer "how good is it?".  Performance scenarios each have a budget; anything not yet met is tracked, and regressions fail.  The web build has a size gate.  The count of live menu commands has a floor.  The scorecard is generated from all of this, and CI fails if the committed copy is stale.

Underneath, every change passes formatting, lint with warnings as errors, the layer checker, and the cross-target builds.  Workers run the narrow checks while they iterate, and the full relevant set before they hand off.
:::

## Fast does not mean finished

```{=html}
<div class="honesty-stage">
  <div class="maturity-board artifact">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>capability scorecard</span><span>evidence, not optimism</span></div>
    <div class="maturity-row"><span>Surface</span><div><i style="width: 94%"></i></div><b>known</b></div>
    <div class="maturity-row"><span>Behavior</span><div><i style="width: 68%"></i></div><b>tested</b></div>
    <div class="maturity-row"><span>Edge cases</span><div><i style="width: 43%"></i></div><b>partial</b></div>
    <div class="maturity-row"><span>Performance</span><div><i style="width: 31%"></i></div><b>measured</b></div>
    <div class="maturity-row"><span>Readiness</span><div><i style="width: 22%"></i></div><b>honest</b></div>
  </div>
  <div class="honesty-copy">
    <div class="eyebrow">BREADTH ≠ DEPTH</div>
    <p class="big-claim compact">A capability can exist without being mature.</p>
    <div class="paired-stat"><b>Surface</b><span>Can it be reached?<br><small>catalog + command</small></span></div>
    <div class="paired-stat warning"><b>Depth</b><span>Can it survive reality?<br><small>fixtures + budgets + edge cases</small></span></div>
    <p>Do not let a busy swarm manufacture confidence faster than software.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Swarming can produce astonishing breadth quickly.  That makes honest maturity tracking essential.

The scorecard separates existence from depth.  A command may be wired and reachable while its edge cases, performance budgets, platform coverage, or recovery paths remain incomplete.

That is useful information, not an embarrassment.  It prevents feature counts from being mistaken for readiness and gives the next wave of workers something concrete to improve.
:::
